Gandhi for Gen Z: The Mahatma is suddenly cool again | A documentary by The Hindu
items.summary: Is Gandhi still relevant to Gen Z? In the summer of 2026, a generation that never studied Mahatma Gandhi sat down at Jantar Mantar, refused to fight back, and unexpectedly rediscovered the power of non-violent resistance. What began as a protest against the NEET paper leak soon raised larger questions about dissent, democracy and the language of political action. As students organised sit-ins, fasts and peaceful demonstrations, echoes of satyagraha surfaced in places where few were consciously looking for Gandhi. From the Cockroach Janata Party’s unconventional movement to grassroots community work led by SEWA, this documentary follows the many ways Gandhian ideas continue to appear in contemporary India. Along the way, it explores the intersections and tensions between Gandhi and Ambedkar, the meaning of civil disobedience in the digital age, and the challenge of practising non-violence in an increasingly polarised society. Featuring Gopalkrishna Gandhi, Ramachandra Guha, Tushar Arun Gandhi, Saurav Das and Mirai Chatterjee, the film brings together historians, activists and organisers to examine Gandhi not as a monument of the past, but as a proposition for the present. This is not a film about what Gandhi said. It is a film about what happens when a new generation unknowingly begins asking the same questions.

items.title: TV Newsance 353: Delhi to Mumbai, everyone wants Gyanesh gone
items.summary: This week on TV Newsance, the streets of Delhi and Mumbai were louder than any prime-time debate. The Cockroach Janta Party’s big contribution to the movement against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was “Gyanesh, it’s done bro.” Meanwhile, Delhi University’s women, out on the streets for women's safety, dropped rhymes that made the men’s slogans look like a draft. Poetry round: Women, 1. Boys, 0. So what lit the match? The Indian Express got hold of the Election Commission’s internal file notings, and they show that the other two commissioners were deeply uncomfortable with how the voter-roll revamp, or SIR, was being run. Two things from those notings remain unexplained: ➨ In West Bengal, 16 lakh appeals were filed against voters being added back to the rolls, and not even the commissioners knew who filed them. ➨ In Goa, 97 eligible voters stayed off the list because the software in Delhi had no “add name” option, despite eight emails begging for one. Yes, the country of software engineers. The government, meanwhile, is busy with the real threat: blocking cartoonists. But in all of this, the worst takes still came from the usual suspects: Godijeevis! They were like “Disagreements happen in every office, bro.” Sure they do, but we’re pretty sure office disagreements differ from a constitutional body like the Election Commission functioning undemocratically. items.title: 30-year-old NOIDA housing dispute: Supreme Court appoints former judge to identify genuine allottees
items.summary: The Supreme Court recently constituted a one-member high-powered independent committee headed by former Allahabad High Court Justice Sudhir Kumar Saxena to finalise the list of genuine members and subsequent purchasers entitled to multi-storeyed flats in NOIDA [ New Okhla Industrial Development Authority v. Kendriya Karamchari Sehkari GN Samiti & Ors. ] A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi , and Justice V Mohana constituted the committee on September 24 after observing that the verification process remained deadlocked despite repeated affidavits and directions. "Having regard to the fact that this process has remained inconclusive despite repeated affidavits and directions and considering that a large number of the original allottee-members have been awaiting the fruits of litigation for over three decades, we are satisfied that an independent verification mechanism to decide the competing claims and implement this Court’s earlier directions is necessary, " the Court ordered. CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana The dispute stemmed from a long sequence of litigation concerning the Kendriya Karamchari Sehkari GN Samiti. In 2022, the top court had directed the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) to allot multi-storeyed flats to 844 identified members of the Society, while ordering the claims of 133 subsequent purchasers to be examined. However, subsequent applications led to conflicting claims between NOIDA and the Society over the exact figures of original members and subsequent buyers, with revised counts fluctuating to 863 original allottees and 120 subsequent purchasers. NOIDA resisted including subsequent purchasers, contending that original allotment letters prohibited transfers without prior permission and pointing out that original allotments were cancelled in 1998. Conversely, the Society argued that NOIDA failed to act on transfer requests and noted that refund cheques were never encashed. Taking note of the continuing stalemate three years after its initial judgment, the Court authorised Justice Saxena to determine his own procedure, examine records, and hear the claimants to conclude the verification. items.title: Baththa: Balaji Tharaneetharan’s Vijay Sethupathi-starrer is powered by a big heart
items.summary: At its core, Balaji Tharaneetharan’s Baththa is a story of love and redemption. Of how, two contrasting people separated by age, power and position can be put together in a situation and yet return with one’s innocence intact and another’s conscience restored. It helps that Baththa , set in the 1980s, is headlined by an in-form Vijay Sethupathi (Baththa) and Master Sai Prithviraj (Sabari), and written and directed superbly by Balaji Tharaneetharan of Naduvula Konjam Pakkatha Kaanom and Seethakathi fame. What happens when gangster Baththa is locked inside a bathroom by terrified little Sabari? This is the basic premise that Balaji builds on. As is expected from Balaji, what you see is not what you get. He shows you something, but what he intends you to see is the gift you receive when you stay invested enough. Like, for example, the title card. Pay close attention to it, for it resides in your mind and adds to the laughter written into a later scene. In Balaji’s world, the things that cause trouble are interesting, and unlikely — if it was a cricket ball in Naduvula, it is Sabari, the terrified child, here. Because the premise is already set that Baththa is a bloodthirsty rowdy who everyone fears, every other antagonist would have looked smaller. So, why not have a really small child trouble him? The film, Balaji’s third collaboration with Vijay Sethupathi, is mostly taut — I would have removed the typical drunk song though, because this film does not really need it as a crutch. You’re at the edge of your seat when Baththa and Sabari are on screen. A locked school toilet during the summer holidays becomes the perfect place for a person’s ego to crumble, like the humble porai (rusk) that he is given to eat. By now everyone knows that if Vijay Sethupathi is given a role of substance, he will walk to the winning post without much effort. That’s what happens in this film. The surprise is Sai Prithviraj, who charms with his vivid portrayal of a frightened child with a conscience. A huge pat on the back for the casting director — from where did he manage to find so many wide-eyed kids oozing innocence and the sparkle of childhood? In a film, sometimes, more than the what and the where, the why is important. In this, Balaji reserves it for the last, and, as a result, you look at Baththa with renewed compassion. items.summary: In this week’s South Central, hosts Pooja Prasanna and Anisha Sheth are joined by political economist and author Dr Parakala Prabhakar for an extended conversation on the Election Commission of India (ECI), the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the deletion of voters and the larger questions these developments raise about India’s electoral democracy. Prabhakar describes the investigation as a significant piece of journalism and argues that the Election Commission’s response did not adequately address several of the specific questions raised by the report, including issues surrounding Form 6 applications, the inclusion of voters and the deletion of names from electoral rolls. He also points to objections and notes reportedly raised by the other two Election Commissioners, questioning why these concerns were not addressed. The conversation then turns to the functioning of the three-member Election Commission and the role of the Chief Election Commissioner. Dr Prabhakar says that the three Election Commissioners have equal status and that the Chief Election Commissioner is “first among equals”, rather than being the supreme authority within the Commission. The discussion then moves to the Election Commission’s claim that the Special Intensive Revision has been endorsed by the Supreme Court. Prabhakar questions the extent of that endorsement, particularly in relation to changes made to Form 6 after the court’s decision. He also asks whether the scale of deletions is consistent with India’s growing population and argues that the process deserves greater scrutiny. items.title: Meta blocks Malayalam digital media NOCAP’s Facebook page after notice
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Meta India has banned the Facebook page of NOCAP, an independent Malayalam digital media organisation in Kerala. According to NOCAP, Meta has explained that the action was taken based on a notice, citing “unlawful activity.” The page was blocked following a notice, said to be issued by the Government of India/Law Enforcement to Meta under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000. It is unclear which law enforcement agency or government including the Union and state governments the notice is from. Ali Hyder, the executive editor of NOCAP, said neither Meta nor the government has so far provided a clear explanation as to which specific content published by NOCAP was deemed “unlawful.” Ali Hyder added that attempts are being made in Kerala to control media organisations and digital platforms that raise voices of dissent against the government through various means. “In this context, the action against NOCAP must be examined seriously,” he said. “NOCAP seeks to use journalism to uphold constitutional values and remain firmly rooted in democratic and secular principles. How can journalism that questions the wrongful tendencies of governments and holds those in power accountable be considered unlawful?” a NOCAP press release notes. The press note also mentioned that a restriction imposed on the voice of one media organisation today must not become a precursor to tampering with the freedom of expression of every citizen tomorrow. This is not the first time that Meta has blocked NOCAP. Earlier in February this year, Meta blocked the Instagram account of NOCAP along with the Malayalam newspaper Deshabhimani, the mouthpiece of the Communist Party of India (Marxist). Following the block, both media outlets began new Instagram handles.
